sources.cite: Microsoft Learn, Restore a database from a backup in Azure SQL Database
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Relevant text: a point-in-time restore 'creates a new database on the same server as the original database'; 'You can't overwrite an existing database during restore'; recovery time depends on size, compute, log volume and activity to replay; to recover from user error either restore and swap names with ALTER DATABASE, or 'write and run a data recovery script that extracts the data from the restored database and applies it to the original'. That a swap loses every change made after the restore point follows from the page (it is not stated there). The az sql db restore flags (--dest-name, --time in ISO 8601) match the 'Restore a single database to an earlier point in time' CLI sample (read 2026-11-18).

brief.situation: You are the database administrator at Haldane Freight. At 14:02 a release script meant for the test database ran against production (Azure SQL Database ops) and truncated dbo.Rates, 48,000 freight rates. Quoting now fails for every lane, but bookings, tracking and invoicing keep writing to other tables in the same database. The 15:00 carrier rate cut-off needs quotes working.
handover: dbo.Rates changes only through the weekly rate load; nothing has legitimately changed it today.
The database is 900 GB; a point-in-time restore of it takes about 25 minutes.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the production database, the restore copy and the tables that keep changing.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: what happened at 14:02, how you restored without losing later work, and what prevents it.

parts.label: What
parts.criteria: Uses the audit log for the exact point.
parts.modelAnswer: deploy-svc ran a test script against production: TRUNCATE TABLE dbo.Rates at 14:02:11. Bookings and tracking kept writing afterwards.

parts.label: Restore
parts.criteria: Copy back only the damaged table.
parts.modelAnswer: Restored ops to 14:01 as a new database (it cannot overwrite) and copied dbo.Rates back into production in one transaction. Swapping the copy in would have lost every booking and tracking event after 14:01.

parts.label: Prevent
parts.modelAnswer: deploy-svc lost its production rights; production changes come only from the release stage with approval. The copy was dropped after the totals matched.

bookingsLost.headline: Restore the table, not the database
bookingsLost.body: A point-in-time restore gives a copy of the whole database. When other tables kept changing, copy back only what was damaged; a swap rolls everything back.

cutoffMissed.headline: Start the restore early
cutoffMissed.body: A restore takes time that grows with size. Start it as soon as you know the restore point, and prepare the copy-back while it runs.

tableBack.headline: Good: a point-in-time restore used surgically
tableBack.body: You found the exact statement and time, saw other tables kept changing, restored a copy to just before the damage, copied back only the emptied table, checked quotes and bookings, and blocked the identity that did it.

scoring.modelReasoning: The audit log shows one TRUNCATE at 14:02:11, and other tables kept changing after it. Restore the database to 14:01 as a new copy (Azure SQL cannot overwrite in place) and copy back only dbo.Rates into production, so later bookings stay. Swapping the copy in would roll back every table; waiting for the weekly load misses the cut-off. Then remove the deploy identity's production rights and drop the copy.
